questions.question: Distinguish between mechanical and chemical digestion and give two examples of each.
questions.expected_answer: Mechanical digestion is the physical breakdown of food into smaller pieces without changing the molecules, increasing the surface area for enzymes; examples: chewing by the teeth, rolling by the tongue, churning of the stomach, emulsification of fats by bile. Chemical digestion is the breakdown of large insoluble molecules into small soluble ones by enzymes; examples: amylase digesting starch to maltose, pepsin or trypsin digesting proteins, lipase digesting fats into fatty acids and glycerol.

questions.question: Name the enzyme, its substrate, its product and the place where it acts for amylase, pepsin and lipase.
questions.expected_answer: Amylase: starch to maltose, in the mouth (salivary) and the small intestine (pancreatic). Pepsin: proteins to shorter chains (on the way to amino acids), in the stomach. Lipase: fats to fatty acids and glycerol, in the small intestine (from the pancreas).

questions.question: In an investigation of the effect of temperature on amylase, name the independent, dependent and two controlled variables, and explain the results at 0 °C and 80 °C.
questions.expected_answer: Independent: temperature. Dependent: time taken for starch to disappear (iodine stays yellow-brown). Controlled: e.g. volume and concentration of starch, volume of amylase, pH, interval between tests. At 0 °C digestion is very slow because molecules move and collide less, but the enzyme is not damaged. At 80 °C there is no digestion because the enzyme is denatured: its active site changes shape permanently so the starch no longer fits.
